slide.title: Find Failures in Minutes
slide.body: A row of node boxes, one red with an error mark; arrows to an 'errors' sheet row and an alert bell. Small tag: AI Agents and Automation Workflows · Lesson 13.

scenes.voiceover: Your workflow will fail. An API key will expire. A sheet column will be renamed. The API will be busy for a minute. The question is not if it fails, but whether you find out in five minutes, or five weeks.

slide.title: Four kinds of failure
slide.body: Temporary: timeout, busy API, rate limit → retry · Permanent: wrong key, deleted sheet → a person fixes it · Bad data: one unexpected item (Lesson 6) · Wrong results: caught by testing (Lesson 14) and approval (Lesson 12)

scenes.voiceover: Welcome to the last module. We start by making things reliable. Plan for four kinds of failure. Temporary errors, like a busy API, are usually fixed by trying again. Permanent errors, like a wrong key or a deleted sheet, need a person. Bad data is one item with unexpected content. And wrong results are runs that succeed but give the wrong output. Testing and approval catch those.

slide.title: Layer 1: Retry On Fail
slide.body: A few tries with a wait between them · Use on API calls · Careful with send or pay actions: a failed try may have succeeded

scenes.voiceover: n8n gives you four layers of protection. First, retry on fail, for temporary errors on API calls. But do not retry an action that sends or pays, unless you are sure the failed try did not already succeed.

slide.title: Layer 2: error output
slide.body: Node with two outputs: success → next step; error → 'dead_letter' tab (item ID + error message). Other items keep flowing.

scenes.voiceover: Second, the on error setting. A node can continue and pass a failed item to an error output. That output goes to a dead letter tab, a list of failed items with the error message, while the other items continue.

slide.title: Layers 3 and 4
slide.body: Main workflow fails → Error workflow (Error Trigger) → record row in 'errors' + notify a person (no secrets, no personal data). Separate: 'log' sheet, one row per run: time · items · failures · tokens · status.

scenes.voiceover: Third, an error workflow. It is a separate workflow that starts with an error trigger. When a run fails, it receives the workflow name, the failed node, the message, and a link. It should record the failure in a sheet, and notify a person, with no personal data and no keys in the message. Fourth, a run log, with one row per run, so you can see trends in failures and cost.
Think of a pilot's emergency checklist. It is written calmly before the flight, not invented during a problem. Your retries, error paths and error workflow are that checklist.

screen_steps: Add Google Sheets: append to 'errors' with time, workflow, node, message, execution_url mapped from the Error Trigger output
scenes.voiceover: Let's build it. Petra Dvořák automates reports at an accounting firm in Prague, Czechia. Her classification workflow runs every night. First, she creates a new workflow called Error handler, with an error trigger. It adds a row to an errors tab, with the time, workflow, node, message and link.

screen_steps: Add an email node: 'Workflow X failed at node Y: message. Link: …' to her own address (blurred)
Open the main workflow → Settings → Error workflow: 'Error handler'
scenes.voiceover: Then it sends her a short email: which workflow failed, at which node, the message, and the link. In the main workflow's settings, she selects Error handler as its error workflow.

screen_steps: Claude HTTP Request node → Settings → Retry On Fail: 3 tries, wait between tries
Error output → Google Sheets append to 'dead_letter' with item ID and error message
End of workflow: Google Sheets append to 'log' with counts and total tokens
scenes.voiceover: On the Claude request node, she turns on retry on fail, with three tries and a wait. She sets on error to continue, using the error output, which goes to a dead letter tab. At the end, she adds a log row with counts and total tokens.

screen_steps: Put a fake key in a copy of the credential
Run manually: the Error handler does not start
Activate the schedule and let it run
Show the new 'errors' row and the email with no secrets
Restore the correct key and run again
scenes.on_screen_text: Break it on purpose, then fix
scenes.voiceover: Now she breaks it on purpose, with a wrong API key, and runs it by hand. The error workflow does not start. She checks the documentation. In her release, error workflows run only for triggered runs. So she tests with the active schedule. The error row appears, and the email arrives. Then she restores the correct key.

scenes.on_screen_text: Green with lost data is worse
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to turn on continue on error everywhere, so every run looks green. Then failures disappear silently. Continuing is only safe when the failed item goes somewhere a person checks. A green run with lost data is worse than a red run that sends an alert.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Retries · error outputs + dead-letter tab · error workflow. 2. Record and notify, with no secrets or personal data. 3. One log row per run.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, use retries for temporary errors, error outputs and a dead letter tab for bad items, and an error workflow for failures that stop a run. Second, the error workflow records the failure and notifies a person, without personal data or secrets. Third, keep a run log with one row per run.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will break your workflow with a wrong API key, confirm that the error workflow logs the failure and notifies you, and then fix the key. It takes about forty minutes. In the next lesson, we cover Testing and Evaluating Agents. See you there.
